title: Read the Last Line First
content:
What problem does this solve?
Programs fail in two broad ways: syntax errors (found before running) and runtime errors (found while running). A traceback reports where and why a runtime error happened. Read the final line first for the error type and message, then move upward to your code. Change one likely cause and run again — a new error is new evidence.

Previously in your program
You fixed logic by reading output. Now you will use error types and messages as evidence when a program stops with a traceback.

Basic syntax
  # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
  item = "rope"
  count = 2
  label = item + ": " + count

What actually happens
A NameError means a variable name was never bound. A TypeError often means incompatible types are being combined. IndexError and KeyError come from selecting a missing position or key. A SyntaxError appears before code runs.

When this is useful
Use the error type and the referenced line to focus your inspection. Fix one problem at a time; the next run gives you the next clue.
concepts: Read the final traceback line first
Name the error type and translate its message
Move upward to your code and inspect those values
Fix one cause and run again — new error, new evidence
SyntaxError appears before the program runs

examples.title: Combine a string and integer
examples.explanation: This raises TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. Converting count or using an f-string fixes it.

common_mistakes: Starting at the top of the traceback instead of the final error line
Changing many things at once and losing track of what changed the behavior
Deleting code to hide the error instead of fixing the cause

exercises.title: Where do you start?
exercises.prompt:
You run a script and see:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<student>", line 3, in <module>
    label = item + ": " + count
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

What is the best first step?
choices: Read the final line for the error type/message, then inspect the referenced learner line.
Start at the first traceback line and rewrite every function shown.
Delete the failing line until the program stops reporting errors.
exercises.success_message: Correct — read the final line first, then inspect the values used on your line.
exercises.failure_message: Use the final error line as evidence. Inspect the values on the referenced learner line and change one likely cause.
hints: The final line names the error type and message.
The referenced line is where your inspection should start.
Change one likely cause; a new error is new evidence.

exercises.title: Syntax stops execution
exercises.prompt: Fix the missing colon so the function runs.
exercises.starter_code:
def route_status(ready):
    if ready
        return "Ready"
    return "Review"
hints: SyntaxError means Python could not parse the code.
Add the missing colon after the if condition.
Do not change the function's behavior.

exercises.title: Follow the misspelled name
exercises.prompt: Fix the misspelled local name so both fields are read from the same member dictionary.
hints: NameError points to an unbound variable name.
Use the same parameter name on both sides.
Both fields come from the member dictionary.

tests.message: Use the provided dictionary's name and role.
Do not hardcode names or roles.
Your fix must work for multiple records.

exercises.title: Convert the value for display
exercises.prompt: Fix the TypeError by converting the count to text (f-string or str(count)).
exercises.starter_code:
def supply_label(item, count):
    return item + ": " + count
hints: You cannot concatenate a string and an integer directly.
Use an f-string or convert count to text with str(count).

tests.message: Do not hardcode — format the provided values.

tests.name: supply_label
tests.message: Define supply_label(item, count) with those two parameters in that order.

exercises.title: One error at a time
exercises.prompt: The first run raises IndexError. Correcting that reveals KeyError. Repair both so the function returns the second member's "health".
exercises.starter_code:
def second_health(party):
    return party[2]["hp"]

party = [
    {"name": "Mira", "health": 8},
    {"name": "Rook", "health": 10},
]

print(second_health(party))
hints: Index 2 is the third element; the second member is at index 1.
The key for health is "health", not "hp".
Fix one cause and run again to see the next clue.

tests.message: After the repairs, the demonstration should print 10.
Return the second member's health for a different two-member party.
Even in a longer party, still select index 1.
